title: A level Paper 2 mock — Set B: The national and global economy
description: A full-length Paper 2 mock covering Themes 2 and 4, with a data response on a fictional emerging economy whose FDI-led growth has raised incomes but also inequality, and an EITHER/OR essay on trading blocs and exchange rate systems. Allow 2 hours: about 25 minutes for Section A, 55 minutes for Section B and 40 minutes for Section C. Show all working in calculations, refer to specific figures from Table 1 and the extracts in every Section B answer, and finish each evaluation question with a justified judgement.

questions.prompt: Over the last year an economy's real GDP growth has slowed from 3.0% to 0.5%, unemployment has started to rise, business confidence has fallen and inflation remains above target. Which phase of the trade cycle best describes the economy?
options: A Boom
B Downturn
C Recession
D Recovery
questions.explanation: In a downturn (slowdown), growth falls but remains positive, confidence weakens and unemployment begins to rise; inflation often lags behind and stays high for a while. A recession (C) requires real GDP to fall, commonly defined as two consecutive quarters of negative growth. A boom (A) has rapid growth and falling unemployment, while recovery (D) involves accelerating growth after a recession.

questions.prompt: In one year, average wages in Country Z rise by 5% and labour productivity rises by 2%. Wages, productivity and prices in its trading partners are unchanged, as is the exchange rate. Which of the following is most likely?
options: A Unit labour costs in Country Z fall by about 3%, improving its international competitiveness
B Unit labour costs in Country Z rise by about 3%, reducing its international competitiveness
C Unit labour costs in Country Z rise by about 7%, reducing its international competitiveness
D International competitiveness is unchanged because productivity has risen
questions.explanation: Unit labour costs are labour costs per unit of output, so they change by roughly the change in wages minus the change in productivity: 5% − 2% ≈ 3% (more precisely 1.05 ÷ 1.02 − 1 = 2.9%). With trading partners' costs and the exchange rate unchanged, Country Z's relative unit labour costs rise, so its international competitiveness falls.

questions.prompt: According to the quantity theory of money (MV = PY), if the money supply grows by 8%, the velocity of circulation is constant and real output grows by 3%, the price level will rise by approximately
questions.explanation: In growth-rate form, %ΔM + %ΔV ≈ %ΔP + %ΔY. With V constant, 8% ≈ %ΔP + 3%, so prices rise by about 5%. Monetarists argue that if the money supply grows faster than real output, the result is inflation.

options: A tax revenue always rises when tax rates rise
B above a certain tax rate, a further increase in the rate may reduce total tax revenue
C a progressive tax system always raises more revenue than a proportional one
D cutting any tax rate always increases total tax revenue
questions.explanation: The Laffer curve shows tax revenue rising with the tax rate up to a revenue-maximising rate, then falling as higher rates reduce incentives to work, invest and declare income, and increase avoidance and evasion. Cutting rates only raises revenue if the rate is above the revenue-maximising point (so D is wrong), and the position of that point is uncertain.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of a market-orientated strategy to promote economic growth and development?
options: A A state-owned development bank providing subsidised loans to industries chosen by the government
B Tariffs on imported manufactured goods to protect infant industries
C Removing restrictions on foreign direct investment and privatising state-owned utilities
D A buffer stock scheme to stabilise the price of a primary export
questions.explanation: Market-orientated strategies rely on free markets and private enterprise: trade liberalisation, promotion of FDI, privatisation and removal of government controls. A, B and D are interventionist strategies, in which the government directs resources, protects industries or manages prices.

questions.prompt: With the aid of an AD/AS diagram, explain why, according to the classical (free-market) view, an increase in aggregate demand has no lasting effect on real output.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: In the classical view, the LRAS curve is vertical at the full-employment (potential) level of real output, determined by the quantity and quality of factors of production, not by the price level.
Diagram: Price level on the vertical axis, real national output on the horizontal axis; vertical LRAS at Yfe; initial equilibrium where AD1 and SRAS1 meet on LRAS; AD shifts right to AD2; SRAS shifts left to SRAS2; new long-run equilibrium on LRAS at a higher price level.
Analysis: The increase in AD initially raises output above Yfe along SRAS1 and raises the price level. With unemployment below its natural rate, labour shortages push up money wages and other input costs, and workers seek higher wages to restore their real wages. Rising costs shift SRAS left until output returns to Yfe. The long-run result is a higher price level with no change in real output: AD changes only cause inflation in the long run.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for an accurate diagram with vertical LRAS and a rightward shift of AD; 1 mark for explaining the short-run rise in output and price level; 1 mark for explaining rising wages and costs shifting SRAS left; 1 mark for explaining the return to full-employment output at a higher price level.

questions.prompt: Explain the likely effects of an import quota on domestic producers and domestic consumers of a good.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: An import quota is a physical limit on the quantity (or value) of a good that may be imported during a period.
Application: For example, a limit on the number of imported cars or tonnes of imported sugar.
Analysis:
- By restricting imports, the quota reduces total supply in the domestic market, so the domestic price rises above the world price.
- Domestic producers: they sell more at a higher price, so their output, revenue, producer surplus and employment rise. However, protection may reduce the incentive to cut costs and innovate (dynamic inefficiency).
- Domestic consumers: they pay higher prices, consume less and have less choice, so consumer surplus falls. Low-income households may be hit hardest if the good is a necessity.
- Unlike a tariff, the government raises no revenue; the gain from the higher price (quota rent) goes to foreign exporters or to holders of import licences.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for defining a quota; 1 mark for explaining why the domestic price rises; 1 mark for a developed effect on domestic producers; 1 mark for a developed effect on domestic consumers.

questions.prompt: Explain how a recession in the UK's main trading partners is likely to affect UK aggregate demand.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Aggregate demand is AD = C + I + G + (X − M). Net trade (X − M) is a component of AD. Exports depend on the real incomes of other countries.
Application: The EU and the USA are the UK's largest export markets, so a recession there (falling real incomes) reduces demand for UK goods and services such as cars, machinery, financial services and tourism.
Analysis: Lower incomes abroad mean fewer UK exports, so X falls and net trade worsens, shifting AD to the left. The fall in exports is a withdrawal of injections from the circular flow, and through the multiplier process, lower incomes for UK exporters and their workers reduce consumption, so the eventual fall in AD and real output is larger than the initial fall in exports. Firms may also cut investment as expected demand falls (accelerator) and confidence weakens.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for knowledge (net trade as a component of AD, or exports depending on foreign incomes); 1 mark for application to the UK context; up to 2 marks for analysis (1 for the fall in exports shifting AD left; 1 for a further developed effect such as the multiplier or the impact on investment or confidence).

questions.prompt: Explain two reasons why absolute poverty may fall in a developing economy at the same time as relative poverty rises.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Absolute poverty is when household income is below the level needed to afford basic needs such as food, shelter and clothing (internationally, the World Bank's extreme poverty line is around $3 a day at purchasing power parity, as updated in 2025). Relative poverty is when income is below a proportion of the median, commonly 60% of median household income.
Application and analysis (any two, developed):
- Rapid economic growth raises the incomes of almost all households, lifting many above the fixed absolute poverty line, but if the incomes of middle and high earners grow faster, the median rises faster than the incomes of the poorest, so more households fall below 60% of the median.
- Growth concentrated in urban, industrial or export sectors raises incomes there much faster than in rural agriculture; rural households may escape absolute poverty but fall further behind.
- Rising returns to skills and education (a skills premium) mean skilled workers' wages rise fastest, widening the gap with unskilled workers even though both are better off.
- Returns to capital rise faster than wages, benefiting asset owners.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: Up to 2 marks for each reason: 1 mark for identifying a reason and 1 mark for explaining why it reduces absolute poverty while increasing relative poverty. Maximum 4 marks. An answer that defines both terms accurately but gives only one reason can score a maximum of 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why the long-run Phillips curve may be vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: The natural rate of unemployment (NAIRU) is the rate of unemployment at which inflation is stable, when the labour market is in equilibrium; it includes frictional and structural unemployment. The short-run Phillips curve shows an inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation.
Analysis:
- Suppose the government uses expansionary policy to reduce unemployment below the natural rate. Higher AD raises prices, and firms hire more workers; in the short run, workers accept money wage rises that do not fully match inflation (money illusion), so unemployment falls and inflation rises along the short-run Phillips curve.
- Workers then revise their inflation expectations upwards and demand higher money wages to restore their real wages. Firms' real labour costs rise, so they reduce employment and unemployment returns to the natural rate, but at the new, higher expected rate of inflation; the short-run Phillips curve shifts up.
- Repeated attempts to hold unemployment below the natural rate lead only to accelerating inflation. In the long run there is no trade-off: any rate of inflation is consistent with the natural rate, so the long-run Phillips curve is vertical.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for defining the natural rate or NAIRU; 1 mark for explaining the short-run trade-off; 1 mark for explaining adjustment of inflation expectations and wages; 1 mark for concluding that unemployment returns to the natural rate at a higher inflation rate, so the long-run curve is vertical. A correct diagram may be credited in place of one written point.

questions.prompt: With reference to Table 1, calculate the percentage change in Taravia's real GDP per capita between 2015 and 2025, and explain why this measure is more useful than the change in nominal GDP for assessing changes in living standards.
questions.context:
Taravia: growth, globalisation and who gains (illustrative data)

Table 1: Selected indicators for Taravia, 2015-2025 (illustrative data)
Year | Nominal GDP (T$ billion) | GDP deflator (2015 = 100) | Population (million) | FDI inflows (% of GDP) | Manufactured goods (% of exports) | Gini coefficient | HDI
2015 | 200 | 100 | 50.0 | 2.1 | 24 | 0.36 | 0.640
2020 | 330 | 125 | 53.0 | 4.8 | 41 | 0.41 | 0.676
2025 | 520 | 160 | 55.0 | 5.6 | 57 | 0.45 | 0.702

Extract A: The factory of the region
Ten years ago the fictional emerging economy of Taravia relied mainly on agriculture and mining. In 2015 the government created three special economic zones (SEZs) on the coast, cutting corporation tax for firms located there from 30% to 12% and removing limits on foreign ownership. It also borrowed to build a new deep-water container port. In 2016 Taravia signed a free trade agreement giving it tariff-free access to a large neighbouring trading bloc.

Multinational electronics and car-parts companies moved assembly plants to the SEZs, attracted by wages around a quarter of those in the region's richer economies, a young workforce and the new port. Manufactured goods rose from 24% to 57% of Taravia's exports. Since 2015 around 2.5 million workers have moved from farms in the inland provinces to jobs in the coastal cities, where output per worker is several times higher than in agriculture.

Extract B: Unequal gains
Real wages in the SEZs have risen by around 6% a year, but incomes in the inland provinces, where two-thirds of the population still live, have grown much more slowly. Most managerial and engineering jobs in foreign-owned plants are filled by staff from abroad or by graduates from the capital. Few Taravian firms supply components to the foreign-owned plants, which import most of their inputs. The government estimates that profits sent home by foreign-owned firms now equal about 4% of GDP each year.

Air pollution in the main port city regularly exceeds safe limits. Tax revenue is only 14% of GDP, and spending on public health and on rural schools has not kept pace with population growth. The share of the population living below the national absolute poverty line has fallen, but surveys show growing resentment in rural areas.

Extract C: Taking back control?
A new government has proposed three measures:
- raising corporation tax in the SEZs from 12% to 20%
- requiring foreign-owned firms to buy at least 40% of their components from Taravian suppliers (a local content rule) and to train local engineers
- adopting the internationally agreed 15% global minimum tax on the profits of large multinational companies.
Investors' groups warn that several firms are considering moving to neighbouring countries where wages are now lower than in Taravia. The government argues that the extra revenue is needed to fund rural schools, health care and pollution controls.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Real GDP removes the effect of inflation: real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ (GDP deflator ÷ 100). Real GDP per capita = real GDP ÷ population.
Application: Real GDP in 2025 (2015 prices) = 520 ÷ 1.60 = T$325 billion. Real GDP in 2015 = T$200 billion. Real GDP per capita: 2015 = 200 ÷ 50.0 = T$4,000; 2025 = 325 ÷ 55.0 = T$5,909 (approximately). Percentage change = (5,909 − 4,000) ÷ 4,000 × 100 = +47.7% (accept 47.7% to 48%).
Analysis: Nominal GDP rose by 160% (from 200 to 520), but most of this reflects rising prices: the deflator rose by 60%, so the volume of goods and services rose much less. The population also grew by 10%, so output had to be shared among more people. Real GDP per capita adjusts for both, so it gives a much better indication of the average quantity of goods and services available per person.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for calculating real GDP in 2025 (T$325bn); 1 mark for both real GDP per capita figures; 1 mark for the correct percentage change of about 47.7% (own-figure rule applies); up to 2 marks for explaining why the measure is better, with 1 mark for adjusting for inflation and 1 mark for adjusting for population growth, ideally using the figures.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge/Application: Economic growth is an increase in real GDP; actual growth may come from increases in AD, while long-run (potential) growth comes from increases in the quantity or quality of factors of production (shifts in LRAS). Real GDP rose from T$200 billion to T$325 billion (2015 prices), an increase of about 62%.
Analysis (any two causes, developed):
- Foreign direct investment: FDI inflows rose from 2.1% to 5.6% of GDP. FDI is an injection that raises AD directly (I), with a multiplier effect, and adds to the capital stock and technology, raising productivity and shifting LRAS right.
- Export-led growth: the free trade agreement gave tariff-free access to a large market, and manufactured goods rose from 24% to 57% of exports. Rising exports raise AD and allow economies of scale.
- Structural change and labour reallocation: 2.5 million workers moved from agriculture to manufacturing where output per worker is several times higher, so average productivity rose.
- Infrastructure: the deep-water port reduced transport costs and raised the economy's productive capacity.
- Low corporation tax in the SEZs (12%) raised post-tax returns, encouraging investment.
Evaluation: Relative significance, for example: FDI is probably the key driver because it underpins both exports and structural change, but it is footloose. Growth built on low wages may not be sustainable as wages rise (wages are now lower in neighbouring countries). Profit repatriation of about 4% of GDP means GNI has grown more slowly than GDP. The data do not allow us to separate the effects precisely.
Levels (KAA up to 6 marks; Evaluation up to 2 marks):
KAA Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated knowledge or definitions; little use of the information provided; analysis is assertion with no chain of reasoning.
KAA Level 2 (3-4 marks): Accurate knowledge with some use of the data; chains of reasoning are developed for one cause or are partial for both.
KAA Level 3 (5-6 marks): Precise knowledge applied to specific figures and evidence from the extracts; two clear, well-linked chains of reasoning.
Evaluation Level 1 (1 mark): A generic or unsupported evaluative comment.
Evaluation Level 2 (2 marks): A supported evaluative comment, for example on relative significance or sustainability, that draws on the data.
A* answer: Selects two distinct causes, uses specific figures (FDI 2.1% to 5.6% of GDP; manufactures 24% to 57% of exports; 2.5 million workers moving), explains each through AD and LRAS with clear chains, and adds a supported judgement about which was more important or how sustainable the growth is.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Income inequality refers to the uneven distribution of income between households. The Gini coefficient measures this, from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality), and is the ratio of the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve to the whole area below the line of equality. The Kuznets curve suggests inequality rises in the early stages of development and falls later.
Application: The Gini coefficient rose from 0.36 in 2015 to 0.45 in 2025, while real GDP per capita rose by about 48%.
Analysis:
- Regional divide: growth is concentrated in the coastal SEZs, where real wages rose about 6% a year, while two-thirds of the population live inland where incomes grew slowly.
- Skills premium: managerial and engineering jobs go to foreign staff or graduates from the capital, so skilled workers gain more than unskilled ones.
- Returns to capital: profits of foreign-owned firms rise; low corporation tax (12%) means owners of capital capture a large share of the gains.
- Weak redistribution: tax revenue of only 14% of GDP limits spending on health, schools and benefits, so the state cannot offset rising market inequality.
- Weak linkages: few Taravian firms supply the foreign plants, so the gains do not spread through the domestic economy.
- Kuznets curve: the shift of labour from low-productivity agriculture to high-productivity industry initially widens inequality.
Evaluation:
- Rising inequality does not mean the poor are worse off: absolute poverty has fallen and HDI has risen.
- The Kuznets curve suggests inequality may fall as more workers move to the modern sector and wages rise, although the evidence for this is mixed.
- The Gini coefficient is a single summary figure: it does not show whether the gains went to the top 10% or the middle, and it ignores wealth inequality and non-market income such as subsistence farming.
- The data are for only three years and may be affected by measurement problems in rural areas.
Levels (KAA up to 6 marks; Evaluation up to 4 marks):
KAA Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated knowledge; little or no reference to the information provided; analysis is descriptive.
KAA Level 2 (3-4 marks): Accurate knowledge with some use of the data; analysis develops relevant chains of reasoning but they are incomplete.
KAA Level 3 (5-6 marks): Precise knowledge applied throughout to the data and extracts; analysis develops clear, logical chains of reasoning, using concepts such as the Lorenz curve or Kuznets curve accurately where relevant.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-2 marks): Generic evaluative comments that are asserted rather than supported.
Evaluation Level 2 (3-4 marks): Evaluation that is supported by the data and context, for example on the limitations of the Gini coefficient or whether the trend will continue.
A* answer: Uses the Gini figures and extract evidence to develop at least two distinct causes (for example, the regional divide and the skills premium) into full chains, links them to the structure of FDI-led growth, and evaluates whether rising inequality is a temporary feature of development or a problem that requires policy, noting the limits of the Gini coefficient.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Economic development is a broad improvement in living standards and welfare, including health, education, freedom and choice, not just higher income. The Human Development Index (HDI) combines life expectancy, education (mean and expected years of schooling) and GNI per capita (PPP).
Application: HDI rose from 0.640 to 0.702, moving Taravia into the UN's "high human development" category (0.700 and above). Real GDP per capita rose by about 48%. Absolute poverty has fallen. Manufactured goods rose from 24% to 57% of exports, reducing dependence on primary products.
Analysis (evidence of improvement): higher real incomes increase access to food, housing and consumer goods; HDI shows broader gains in health and education; structural change towards manufacturing reduces exposure to volatile primary commodity prices and develops skills and infrastructure; rising real wages in the SEZs.
Analysis (evidence against): inequality has widened (Gini up from 0.36 to 0.45), so gains are unevenly shared; profit repatriation of about 4% of GDP means GNI and national income have grown more slowly than GDP; air pollution in the port city damages health; spending on rural schools and health has not kept pace with population growth; dependence on footloose foreign firms with few local linkages.
Evaluation:
- HDI is an average and does not capture distribution, environmental damage or political freedoms; an inequality-adjusted HDI would show smaller gains.
- The rise in HDI is modest relative to the 48% rise in real income, suggesting income gains have not fully translated into health and education.
- Whether development is sustainable depends on whether firms stay as wages rise and whether the government can raise revenue to invest in human capital.
- Judgement: there has been genuine but uneven development, strong in income and structural change, weaker in distribution, environment and public services, with some doubt about sustainability.
Levels (KAA up to 8 marks; Evaluation up to 4 marks):
KAA Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated or partially accurate knowledge; little use of the information provided; analysis is absent or a list of assertions.
KAA Level 2 (3-5 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; one or two developed chains of reasoning, which may be one-sided.
KAA Level 3 (6-8 marks): Precise knowledge applied consistently to the data; several clear, logical chains of reasoning covering both the evidence of improved development and the evidence against it.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-2 marks): Generic evaluation that is asserted rather than supported.
Evaluation Level 2 (3-4 marks): Balanced evaluation, supported by evidence from Table 1 and the extracts, leading to a judgement on the extent of development.
A* answer: Uses several indicators from Table 1 (HDI, real GDP per capita, Gini, export structure) and extract evidence (pollution, profit repatriation, rural services), explains why each indicates or fails to indicate development, recognises the limitations of HDI and GDP-based measures, and reaches a balanced judgement on the extent and sustainability of development.

Extract A: The factory of the region
Ten years ago the fictional emerging economy of Taravia relied mainly on agriculture and mining. In 2015 the government created three special economic zones (SEZs) on the coast, cutting corporation tax for firms located there from 30% to 12% and removing limits on foreign ownership. It also borrowed to build a new deep-water container port. In 2016 Taravia signed a free trade agreement giving it tariff-free access to a large neighbouring trading bloc.

Multinational electronics and car-parts companies moved assembly plants to the SEZs, attracted by wages around a quarter of those in the region's richer economies, a young workforce and the new port. Manufactured goods rose from 24% to 57% of Taravia's exports. Since 2015 around 2.5 million workers have moved from farms in the inland provinces to jobs in the coastal cities, where output per worker is several times higher than in agriculture.

Extract B: Unequal gains
Real wages in the SEZs have risen by around 6% a year, but incomes in the inland provinces, where two-thirds of the population still live, have grown much more slowly. Most managerial and engineering jobs in foreign-owned plants are filled by staff from abroad or by graduates from the capital. Few Taravian firms supply components to the foreign-owned plants, which import most of their inputs. The government estimates that profits sent home by foreign-owned firms now equal about 4% of GDP each year.

Air pollution in the main port city regularly exceeds safe limits. Tax revenue is only 14% of GDP, and spending on public health and on rural schools has not kept pace with population growth. The share of the population living below the national absolute poverty line has fallen, but surveys show growing resentment in rural areas.

Extract C: Taking back control?
A new government has proposed three measures:
- raising corporation tax in the SEZs from 12% to 20%
- requiring foreign-owned firms to buy at least 40% of their components from Taravian suppliers (a local content rule) and to train local engineers
- adopting the internationally agreed 15% global minimum tax on the profits of large multinational companies.
Investors' groups warn that several firms are considering moving to neighbouring countries where wages are now lower than in Taravia. The government argues that the extra revenue is needed to fund rural schools, health care and pollution controls.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Multinational corporations (MNCs) operate in more than one country. Government controls include taxation, regulation of transfer pricing, local content rules and requirements on training. Footloose firms can relocate easily. The WTO Agreement on Trade-Related Investment Measures (TRIMs) restricts local content requirements.
Application: Corporation tax in the SEZs is 12%; profits repatriated equal about 4% of GDP; tax revenue is only 14% of GDP; few local firms supply foreign plants; FDI inflows are 5.6% of GDP; wages are now lower in neighbouring countries.
Analysis (case for):
- Higher corporation tax and a 15% minimum tax would raise revenue to fund rural schools, health care and pollution controls, improving human capital and reducing inequality and the negative externalities of production.
- Local content rules create backward linkages, increase demand for domestic suppliers, keep more of the value added in Taravia and help domestic firms gain technology and skills (spillovers).
- Training requirements raise the skills of local workers, enabling them to fill higher-paid jobs and raising productivity (LRAS).
- The global minimum tax limits the "race to the bottom" in which countries compete by cutting tax rates.
Analysis (case against):
- Higher costs reduce post-tax returns, so FDI inflows may fall and some firms may relocate to lower-cost neighbours, cutting jobs, exports and growth (AD falls with a negative multiplier).
- If local suppliers are less efficient, local content rules raise costs and reduce the competitiveness of Taravia's exports.
- Local content rules may breach WTO rules and the terms of the free trade agreement, risking disputes.
- Uncertainty about policy may deter future investment.
Evaluation:
- Elasticity of FDI to tax: firms have made large sunk investments in plant and rely on the port and FTA access, so they may be less footloose than investors' groups claim. Tax is only one factor; access to markets and infrastructure matter.
- The 15% global minimum tax is less likely to cause relocation because neighbouring countries face the same minimum; raising the rate to 20% is riskier.
- Sequencing and phasing: gradual introduction, or using incentives (subsidies for local suppliers, training partnerships) rather than mandates, may achieve linkages without deterring FDI.
- Rising wages mean Taravia must move up the value chain anyway; investment in skills funded by the extra revenue could make it more attractive in the long run.
- Distinguish between the measures: the global minimum tax and training requirements have a strong case; the 40% local content rule is the most risky.
- Judgement: a moderate case for the measures, especially if phased in and targeted, but the government must weigh short-run losses of FDI against long-run gains in revenue and development.
Levels (KAA up to 9 marks; Evaluation up to 6 marks):
KAA Level 1 (1-3 marks): Isolated or partially accurate knowledge; little or no application to the context; analysis consists of unconnected assertions.
KAA Level 2 (4-6 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of data; relevant chains of reasoning are developed but may be incomplete or one-sided.
KAA Level 3 (7-9 marks): Precise knowledge applied consistently to Taravia; clear, logical and well-linked chains of reasoning covering the benefits and costs of the measures.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-2 marks): Generic evaluative comments that are not supported or applied.
Evaluation Level 2 (3-4 marks): Evaluation is present and applied to the context but is not fully developed or does not lead to a clear judgement.
Evaluation Level 3 (5-6 marks): Balanced, well-supported evaluation that distinguishes between the measures, considers short-run and long-run effects and different stakeholders, and reaches a fully justified judgement.
A* answer: Analyses each measure separately with clear chains to revenue, linkages, FDI and growth, uses the data (12% tax, 4% of GDP repatriated, 14% tax revenue, lower wages in neighbouring countries) to judge the likely response of firms, considers WTO constraints and the effect of the global minimum tax on relocation incentives, and reaches a justified judgement that distinguishes between the measures and the time period.

questions.prompt:
Answer EITHER (a) OR (b). Start your answer by writing (a) or (b).

(a) Evaluate whether the economic benefits for a country of joining a customs union are likely to outweigh the economic costs.

(b) Evaluate the view that a floating exchange rate system is better than a fixed exchange rate system for a small open economy.
questions.mark_scheme:
Option (a): costs and benefits of joining a customs union
Knowledge: A customs union is a trading bloc with free trade between members and a common external tariff (CET) on imports from non-members; it differs from a free trade area, where members set their own external tariffs. Trade creation, trade diversion, economies of scale, the WTO.
Application: Examples include the EU customs union (the UK left it at the end of the Brexit transition period in 2020), the EU-Turkey customs union for industrial goods, and Mercosur in South America. UK firms now face rules of origin checks and customs declarations when trading with the EU.
Analysis:
- Trade creation: removing tariffs on trade with members allows a switch from higher-cost domestic production to lower-cost member producers, lowering prices and increasing consumer surplus (tariff diagram showing the gain).
- Larger market: firms gain economies of scale, more competition improves efficiency and innovation, and FDI from outside the bloc may increase as firms locate inside the CET.
- No rules of origin: goods move freely without customs checks, reducing administrative costs and supporting integrated supply chains (for example, cars and components crossing borders several times).
- Collective bargaining power in trade negotiations.
- Costs: trade diversion, where imports switch from a low-cost non-member to a higher-cost member because of the CET, which can reduce welfare; loss of the ability to set an independent trade policy or sign separate trade deals; structural unemployment in domestic industries exposed to competition from members; retaliation by non-members.
Evaluation:
- Net welfare depends on whether trade creation exceeds trade diversion, which depends on the level of the CET, the efficiency of member producers compared with the rest of the world, and how much trade was already with members.
- The benefits are larger for a country whose trade is concentrated within the bloc and that is integrated in regional supply chains.
- Dynamic gains (competition, scale, FDI) tend to be larger in the long run than static gains.
- Loss of trade policy sovereignty matters more for a country with strong trade links outside the bloc or a large services sector (customs unions mainly cover goods).
- The costs fall unevenly across regions and industries; the overall judgement may differ for consumers, producers and workers.

Option (b): floating versus fixed exchange rates for a small open economy
Knowledge: Floating exchange rates are determined by the demand for and supply of the currency; fixed rates are set by the central bank and maintained through intervention (buying and selling reserves) and interest rates; managed float as an intermediate system.
Application: Examples include Denmark, which pegs the krone closely to the euro; Hong Kong, whose currency has been pegged to the US dollar since 1983; and the UK's exit from the Exchange Rate Mechanism in 1992, when it could not defend sterling's fixed rate. Small open economies have high trade shares in GDP.
Analysis (for floating):
- Automatic adjustment: a current account deficit tends to lead to depreciation, making exports cheaper and imports dearer, helping restore balance (subject to Marshall-Lerner).
- Monetary policy independence: interest rates can be used for domestic objectives (inflation, growth) rather than defending the exchange rate.
- No need to hold large foreign currency reserves.
- Absorbs external shocks: depreciation cushions falls in export demand.
Analysis (for fixed):
- Certainty for traders and investors, reducing transaction risk and encouraging trade and FDI; particularly valuable for a small open economy where trade is a large share of GDP.
- Imports anti-inflation credibility from the anchor currency, disciplining domestic policy and lowering inflation expectations.
- Avoids volatility caused by speculation and hot money flows.
- Costs: loss of monetary independence; risk of speculative attack and loss of reserves if the peg is not credible; adjustment to shocks must happen through wages, prices and unemployment instead of the exchange rate.
Evaluation:
- For a small open economy, exchange rate volatility has a large impact on prices and output, which strengthens the case for a fixed or managed rate.
- Floating is better when the economy faces different shocks from its anchor country and needs independent interest rates; a fixed rate works best when the economy's business cycle is closely synchronised with the anchor (Denmark and the euro area).
- Credibility of the peg and the size of reserves are crucial; without them a fixed system can collapse, as in 1992.
- A floating rate's adjustment may be slow or ineffective if demand for imports and exports is price inelastic; depreciation may cause imported inflation.
- A managed float may combine the advantages.
- Judgement depends on the economy's trade pattern, the credibility of its institutions and the type of shocks it faces.

Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis up to 16 marks; Evaluation up to 9 marks.
Levels (KAA up to 16 marks; Evaluation up to 9 marks):
KAA Level 1 (1-4 marks): Isolated knowledge, often definitions only; little application to real economies; analysis is descriptive or confused.
KAA Level 2 (5-8 marks): Accurate knowledge with some relevant application; chains of reasoning are developed for one or two points but are partial or one-sided; diagrams may be present but are not fully explained.
KAA Level 3 (9-12 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to relevant, realistic examples; several developed chains of reasoning with appropriate diagrams (for example a tariff diagram or a currency market diagram).
KAA Level 4 (13-16 marks): Precise, wide-ranging knowledge applied throughout to well-chosen examples; fully developed, logical chains of reasoning with accurate diagrams integrated into the argument.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-3 marks): Generic evaluative comments, asserted rather than supported.
Evaluation Level 2 (4-6 marks): Evaluation is present and partly supported, considering alternative outcomes, but is not consistently developed or prioritised.
Evaluation Level 3 (7-9 marks): Sustained evaluation throughout that weighs arguments, considers the type of economy, time period and magnitude, and reaches a fully justified overall judgement.
A* answer: For (a), uses a tariff diagram to explain trade creation and trade diversion precisely, brings in dynamic gains and the loss of trade policy sovereignty with real examples (EU, Turkey, Mercosur, UK after Brexit), and judges that the net effect depends on the CET, existing trade patterns and the structure of the economy. For (b), develops the adjustment, policy independence, certainty and credibility arguments with real examples (Denmark, Hong Kong, the UK in 1992), applies them specifically to a small open economy, and reaches a reasoned judgement on the conditions under which each system is better.
